The "for" refers, not to the words immediately preceding, but to the consolations in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Is 8:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.17">10, 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">18</reference>. Do not despair, for, &c.<div eID="gen13708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when at the first, &c.--</hi>rather, "as the former time has brought contempt on the land of Zebulun and Naphtali (namely, the deportation of their inhabitants under Tiglath-pileser, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>, a little before the giving of this prophecy); so shall the after-coming time bring honor to the way of the sea (the district around the lake of Galilee), the land beyond (but Hengstenberg, "by the side of") Jordan (Perea, east of Jordan, belonging to Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh), the circle (but Hengstenberg, "Galilee") (that is, region) of the "Gentiles" [Maurer, Hengstenberg, &c.]. Galil in Hebrew is a "circle," "circuit," and from it came the name Galilee. North of Naphtali, inhabited by a mixed race of Jews and Gentiles of the bordering Phoenician race (<reference osisRef="Judg.1.30">Jud 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.11">1Ki 9:11</reference>). Besides the recent deportation by Tiglath-pileser, it had been sorely smitten by Ben-hadad of Syria, two hundred years before (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.20">1Ki 15:20</reference>). It was after the Assyrian deportation colonized with heathens, by Esar-haddon (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.24">2Ki 17:24</reference>). Hence arose the contempt for it on the part of the southern Jews of purer blood (<reference osisRef="John.1.46">Joh 1:46</reference>; 7:52). The same region which was so darkened once, shall be among the first to receive Messiah's light (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.13">Mt 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.16">15, 16</reference>). It was in despised Galilee that He first and most publicly exercised His ministry; from it were most of His apostles. Foretold in <reference osisRef="Deut.33.18">De 33:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.7">Ac 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.27">Psa 68:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28">28</reference>, Jerusalem, the theocratic capital, might readily have known Messiah; to compensate less favored Galilee, He ministered mostly there; Galilee's very debasement made it feel its need of a Saviour, a feeling not known to the self-righteous Jews (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">Mt 9:13</reference>). It was appropriate, too, that He who was both "the Light to lighten the Gentiles, and the Glory of His people Israel," should minister chiefly on the border land of Israel, near the Gentiles. <div eID="gen13709" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 9 Is 9:1-7 . Continuation of the Prophecy in the Eighth Chapter. 1. Nevertheless, &c.-- rather, "For darkness shall not (continually) be on it (that is, the land) on which there is (now) distress" [Hengstenberg and Maurer]. The "for" refers, not to the words immediately preceding, but to the consolations in Is 8:9 , 10, 17 , 18 . Do not despair, for, &c. when at the first, &c.-- rather, "as the former time has brought contempt on the land of Zebulun and Naphtali (namely, the deportation of their inhabitants under Tiglath-pileser, 2Ki 15:29 , a little before the giving of this prophecy); so shall the after-coming time bring honor to the way of the sea (the district around the lake of Galilee), the land beyond (but Hengstenberg, "by the side of") Jordan (Perea, east of Jordan, belonging to Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh), the circle (but Hengstenberg, "Galilee") (that is, region) of the "Gentiles" [Maurer, Hengstenberg, &c.]. Galil in Hebrew is a "circle," "circuit," and from it came the name Galilee. North of Naphtali, inhabited by a mixed race of Jews and Gentiles of the bordering Phoenician race ( Jud 1:30 ; 1Ki 9:11 ). Besides the recent deportation by Tiglath-pileser, it had been sorely smitten by Ben-hadad of Syria, two hundred years before ( 1Ki 15:20 ). It was after the Assyrian deportation colonized with heathens, by Esar-haddon ( 2Ki 17:24 ). Hence arose the contempt for it on the part of the southern Jews of purer blood ( Joh 1:46 ; 7:52). The same region which was so darkened once, shall be among the first to receive Messiah's light ( Mt 4:13 , 15, 16 ). It was in despised Galilee that He first and most publicly exercised His ministry; from it were most of His apostles. Foretold in De 33:18 , 19 ; Ac 2:7 ; Psa 68:27 , 28 , Jerusalem, the theocratic capital, might readily have known Messiah; to compensate less favored Galilee, He ministered mostly there; Galilee's very debasement made it feel its need of a Saviour, a feeling not known to the self-righteous Jews ( Mt 9:13 ). It was appropriate, too, that He who was both "the Light to lighten the Gentiles, and the Glory of His people Israel," should minister chiefly on the border land of Israel, near the Gentiles.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8475"/><div sID="gen13712" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8475"/><hi type="bold">3. multiplied ... nation--</hi>primarily, the rapid increase of Israelites after the return from Babylon; more fully and exhaustively the rapid spread of Christianity at first.<div eID="gen13712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not increased the joy--</hi>By a slight change in the Hebrew, its (joy) is substituted by some for not, because "not increased the joy" seems opposite to what immediately follows, "the joy," &c. Hengstenberg, retains not thus: "Whose joy thou hadst not increased," (that is, hadst diminished). Others, "Hast thou not increased the joy?" The very difficulty of the reading, not, makes it less likely to be an interpolation. Horsley best explains it: The prophet sees in vision a shifting scene, comprehending at one glance the history of the Christian Church to remotest times--a land dark and thinly peopled--lit up by a sudden light--filled with new inhabitants--then struggling with difficulties, and again delivered by the utter and final overthrow of their enemies. The influx of Gentile converts (represented here by "Galilee of the Gentiles") soon was to be followed by the growth of corruption, and the final rise of Antichrist, who is to be destroyed, while God's people is delivered, as in the case of Gideon's victory over Midian, not by man's prowess, but by the special interposition of God.<div eID="gen13713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before thee--</hi>a phrase taken from sacrificial feasts; the tithe of harvest was eaten before God (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.7">De 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.14.26">14:26</reference>).<div eID="gen13714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as men rejoice ... divide ... spoil--</hi>referring to the judgments on the enemies of the Lord and His people, which usually accompany revelations of His grace. <div eID="gen13715" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8476"/><div sID="gen13716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8476"/>4. The occasion of the "joy," the deliverance not only of Ahaz and Judah from the Assyrian tribute (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.8">2Ki 16:8</reference>), and of Israel's ten tribes from the oppressor (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Ki 15:19</reference>), but of the Jewish Christian Church from its last great enemy.<div eID="gen13716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hast--</hi>the past time for the future, in prophetic vision; it expresses the certainty of the event.<div eID="gen13717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yoke of his burden--</hi>the yoke with which he was burdened.<div eID="gen13718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">staff of ... shoulder--</hi>the staff which strikes his shoulder [Maurer]; or the wood, like a yoke, on the neck of slaves, the badge of servitude [Rosenmuller].<div eID="gen13719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13720" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day of Midian--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.7.8-Judg.7.22">Jud 7:8-22</reference>). As Gideon with a handful of men conquered the hosts of Midian, so Messiah the "child" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>) shall prove to be the "Prince of peace," and the small Israel under Him shall overcome the mighty hosts of Antichrist (compare <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2-Mic.5.5">Mi 5:2-5</reference>), containing the same contrast, and alluding also to "the Assyrian," the then enemy of the Church, as here in Isaiah, the type of the last great enemy. For further analogies between Gideon's victory and the Gospel, compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2Co 4:7</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Judg.7.22">Jud 7:22</reference>. As the "dividing of the spoil" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Is 9:3</reference>) was followed by that which was "not joy," the making of the idolatrous ephod (<reference osisRef="Judg.8.24-Judg.8.27">Jud 8:24-27</reference>), so the gospel victory was soon followed by apostasy at the first, and shall be so again after the millennial overthrow of Antichrist (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.3">Re 20:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.20.7-Rev.20.9">7-9</reference>), previous to Satan's last doom (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.10">Re 20:10</reference>). <div eID="gen13720" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8477"/><div sID="gen13721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8477"/><hi type="bold">5. every battle, &c.--</hi>rather, "every greave of (the warrior who is) armed with greaves in the din of battle, and the martial garment (or cloak, called by the Latins sagum) rolled in blood, shall be for burning, (and) fuel for fire" [Maurer]. All warlike accoutrements shall be destroyed, as no longer required in the new era of peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Is 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.6">11:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.46.9">Psa 46:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.9">Eze 39:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.5.5">Mi 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mic.5.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">10</reference>). Compare Mal 4:1, as to the previous burning up of the wicked. <div eID="gen13721" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8478"/><div sID="gen13722" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8478"/><hi type="bold">6. For--</hi>the ground of these great expectations,<div eID="gen13722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto us--</hi>for the benefit of the Jews first, and then the Gentiles (compare "unto you," <reference osisRef="Luke.2.11">Lu 2:11</reference>).<div eID="gen13723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son ... given--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.2.7">Psa 2:7</reference>). God's gratuitous gift, on which man had no claim (<reference osisRef="John.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.6.23">Ro 6:23</reference>).<div eID="gen13724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">government ... upon ... shoulder--</hi>The ensign of office used to be worn on the shoulder, in token of sustaining the government (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.22">Is 22:22</reference>). Here the government on Messiah's shoulder is in marked antithesis to the "yoke and staff" of the oppressor on Israel's "shoulder" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.4">Is 9:4</reference>). He shall receive the kingdom of the earth from the Father, to vindicate it from the misrule of those to whom it was entrusted to hold it for and under the Most High, but who sought to hold it in defiance of His right; the Father asserts His right by the Son, the "Heir of all things," who will hold it for Him (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Da 7:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen13725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">name ... called--</hi>His essential characteristics shall be.<div eID="gen13726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Wonderful--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.8.18">Is 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.13.18">Jud 13:18</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen13727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Counsellor--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">Psa 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.34">34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.24">1Co 1:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.3">Col 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen13728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.10.21">Is 10:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.8">Psa 24:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>) Horsley translates: "God the mighty man." "Unto us ... God" is equivalent to "Immanuel" (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Is 7:14</reference>).<div eID="gen13729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting Father--</hi>This marks Him as "Wonderful," that He is "a child," yet the "everlasting Father" (<reference osisRef="John.10.30">Joh 10:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.9">14:9</reference>). entries.content_plain: 6. For-- the ground of these great expectations, unto us-- for the benefit of the Jews first, and then the Gentiles (compare "unto you," Lu 2:11 ). son ... given-- ( Psa 2:7 ). God's gratuitous gift, on which man had no claim ( Joh 3:16 ; Ro 6:23 ). government ... upon ... shoulder-- The ensign of office used to be worn on the shoulder, in token of sustaining the government ( Is 22:22 ). Here the government on Messiah's shoulder is in marked antithesis to the "yoke and staff" of the oppressor on Israel's "shoulder" ( Is 9:4 ). Of ... increase ... no end--</hi>His princely rule shall perpetually increase and be unlimited (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.44">Da 2:44</reference>).<div eID="gen13732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">throne of David--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.25">1Ki 8:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Psa 2:6</reference>; 132:11; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">18</reference> Eze 34:23-26; 37:<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.22">16, 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Lu 1:32</reference>, 33; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30">Ac 2:30</reference>).<div eID="gen13733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment ... justice--</hi>It is not a kingdom of mere might, and triumph of force over enemies, but of righteousness (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.21">Is 42:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6">Psa 45:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">7</reference>), attainable only in and by Messiah.<div eID="gen13734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">zeal, &c.--</hi>including not only Christ's hidden spiritual victory over Satan at the first coming, but the open one accompanied with "judgments" on Antichrist and every enemy at the second coming (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Is 59:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.6-Ps.9.8">Psa 9:6-8</reference>).<div eID="gen13735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13736" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8-Isa.10.4">Is 9:8-10:4</reference>. Prophecy as to the Ten Tribes.<div eID="gen13736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13737" type="x-p"/> Delivered a little later than the previous one. The ninth and tenth chapters ought to have been so divided. The present division into chapters was made by Cardinal Hugo, in A.D. 1250; and into verses, by Robert Stephens, the famous printer of Paris, in 1551. After the Assyrian invasion of Syria, that of Ephraim shall follow (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>); Is 9:8-11, 17-20, foretell the intestine discords in Israel after Hoshea had slain Pekah (A.D. 739), that is, just after the Assyrian invasions, when for seven years it was stripped of magistrates and torn into factions. There are four strophes, each setting forth Ephraim's crime and consequent punishment, and ending with the formula, "For all this His anger is not turned away," &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.12">Is 9:12</reference>, 17, 21, and <reference osisRef="Isa.10.4">Is 10:4</reference>). <div eID="gen13737" type="x-p"/>
